title: Can you vacation in Antarctica?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant (Chuck is sick) explore whether you can vacation in Antarctica. They cover Captain Robert Scott's 1911 expedition and its emperor penguin eggs, Antarctica's climate and size, the first people born there (Emilio Marcos de Palma, Juan Pablo Camacho) and the 1959 Antarctic Treaty, how tourists reach the continent by cruise ship from Argentina or Chile, cruise ship safety and groundings, weather delays, Leonid Rogozov's self-performed appendectomy, Kodak Gap, Mount Vinson, the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, marathons, wildlife, tourism regulation, and the Scotch whisky found at Shackleton's hut. The episode ends with listener mail about daylight saving time and a Canadian listener's complaint.

segments.title: Opening banter and Captain Scott's expedition
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with Chuck being sick. They discuss Captain Robert Scott's expedition, which lost the race to the South Pole, the deaths of his team, and the emperor penguin eggs the team collected to test evolutionary theory.

segments.title: Antarctica's geography and climate
segments.summary: The hosts describe Antarctica as the fifth largest continent, mostly ice, with very low temperatures, constant strong winds, and few year-round residents, who live in temporary research stations.

segments.title: Births and sovereignty under the Antarctic Treaty
segments.summary: They discuss the first people born in Antarctica, Emilio Marcos de Palma and Juan Pablo Camacho, the countries that have claimed parts of the continent, and the 1959 Antarctic Treaty that bars claims and military use.

segments.title: Antarctica in fiction and off-topic chat
segments.summary: Brief tangent on H.P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness, possible film adaptations, and a conversation about Spinal Tap and Christopher Guest films.

segments.title: Getting to Antarctica and cruise tourism
segments.summary: Travel to Antarctica is mainly by ship from southern South America to the Antarctic Peninsula. Cruise tourism grew from about 9,000 people a year in the early nineties to about 40,000 in 2007-2008. The IAATO was formed to keep tourism ethical.

segments.title: Cruise ship safety, groundings, and weather delays
segments.summary: Hulls of many cruise ships cannot withstand icebergs. The Lindblad Explorer, the first cruise ship to Antarctica, sank in 2007 (renamed MS Explorer). Four ships have run aground since 2007. Summer weather can strand travelers, and winter travel is impossible.

segments.title: Leonid Rogozov's self-performed appendectomy
segments.summary: Russian surgeon Leonid Rogozov performed an appendectomy on himself at the Novolazarevskaya base during the winter, without anesthesia, after realizing he had appendicitis.

segments.title: Activities: Kodak Gap, Mount Vinson, marathons, South Pole, wildlife
segments.summary: Sightseeing includes cruises through the Kodak Gap, climbing Mount Vinson, cross-country skiing expeditions, and a marathon run by Adventure Network International. Visitors can visit the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. Penguins are unafraid of humans but hosts advise not to disturb them.

segments.title: Costs, environmental concerns, and tourism regulation
segments.summary: A trip may cost around ten thousand dollars. DDT has been found in Antarctic penguins. A 2009 joint Antarctic Treaty and Arctic Council meeting in Baltimore discussed tourism limits after a large ice shelf broke off. Proposed limits include ship numbers and shore distance; the treaty allows freedom of access.

segments.title: Shackleton's Scotch whisky
segments.summary: Eleven bottles of Mackinlay Scotch left by Ernest Shackleton's 1907 Nimrod expedition were found in 2006 and are now held by the Canterbury Museum in Christchurch, New Zealand. Some scotch makers have been allowed to sample it to recreate the recipe.

segments.title: Listener mail on daylight saving time
segments.summary: A listener from White Horse, Yukon, Canada, objected to Josh's comment that time makes no difference in the civilized world. Chuck replies that clocks are a human invention for scheduling, and apologizes for any offense. They also mention Dana Carvey as a listener story prompt.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and invite stories and feedback via Twitter, Facebook, and email, and mention the HowStuffWorks app.
